title: Update on COVID-19 Treatments, Vaccination Efficacy and Roll-out for Children and Booster Jabs
what_it_is: Update on COVID-19 Treatments, Vaccination Efficacy and Roll-out for Children and Booster Jabs

sections.label: Omicron readiness and strategies
sections.summary: Questions ask about Singapore's ability to cope with Omicron, imported case breakdown by country, mitigation strategies, booster doses and anti-viral pills.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health whether the Ministry can provide an update on (i) Singapore’s ability to cope with increasing number of infections arising from the COVID-19 Omicron variant, (ii) the breakdown, by country of origin, for imported COVID-19 Omicron cases and (iii) the strategies to mitigate imported cases.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health with regard to containing the Omicron variant of COVID-19 (a) whether the Ministry has assessed a need for more vaccination doses after the booster jab; and (b) how does the Ministry plan to utilise the anti-viral pills as part of its strategy.

sections.label: Medically ineligible and unvaccinated numbers
sections.summary: Questions ask how many Singaporeans and PRs are medically ineligible for COVID-19 vaccination and how many remain unvaccinated as of December 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health (a) how many Singaporeans and Permanent Residents (PRs) respectively are deemed to be medically ineligible for COVID-19 vaccination; and (b) excluding these persons, how many Singaporeans and PRs respectively remain unvaccinated as of December 2021.

sections.label: ICU capacity and healthcare workers
sections.summary: Questions ask about expected Omicron ICU impact, ICU utilisation rate for deferring non-urgent services, ICU worker numbers and permanent capacity changes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is the expected impact on ICU utilisation based on the Ministry’s modelling for the COVID-19 Omicron variant; (b) at what ICU utilisation rate will hospitals begin to defer non-urgent clinical services; (c) what is the number of healthcare workers working in ICUs currently as compared to December 2020; and (d) what permanent changes have been made to increase healthcare capacity and, in particular, ICU capacity and scalability since (i) the start of the pandemic and (ii) the start of 2021.

sections.label: Stable hospital situation
sections.summary: The hospital situation is stable, with 11 COVID-19-related ICU cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: As of now, our hospital situation is stable, with 11 COVID-19-related ICU cases.

sections.label: Omicron transmissibility and wave size
sections.summary: Omicron is far more transmissible than Delta, and a wave could reach 10,000 to 15,000 cases a day or more.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: First, local and overseas evidence shows that it is far more transmissible than the Delta variant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: We must expect a wave that could be a few times larger than the Delta wave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, if Delta infections reached a sustained incidence of about 3,000 cases a day, Omicron could perhaps reach 10,000 to 15,000 cases a day or even more.

sections.label: Lower hospitalisation and severe illness
sections.summary: Hospitalisation and severe illness incidence is lower, with indications that hospital stays are shorter.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: The incidence of hospitalisation and severe illness is lower and there are also indications that any hospital stays are also shorter.

sections.label: South Africa Omicron hospitalisation study
sections.summary: A South African study found 4.9% of Omicron cases were admitted to hospital versus 13.7% during the Delta wave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: A study by health authorities in South Africa showed that 4.9% of cases were admitted to hospitals during the Omicron wave, compared to 13.7% during the Delta wave.

sections.label: Singapore Omicron infection numbers
sections.summary: Singapore recorded 4,322 Omicron infections, including 308 seniors aged 60 and above, with eight needing oxygen supplementation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: In Singapore, we have recorded 4,322 Omicron infections so far, including 308 seniors aged 60 and above.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Eight of the 4,322 needed oxygen supplementation, and all of them have been taken off oxygen after a short few days.

sections.label: COVID-19 deaths breakdown 2021
sections.summary: Mr Dennis Tan asked for a breakdown of COVID-19 deaths; there were 802 deaths in 2021, of whom 555 were not fully vaccinated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Mr Dennis Tan asked for a breakdown of COVID-19 deaths.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: There were 802 such deaths in 2021, of whom 555 were not fully vaccinated.

sections.label: Crude incidence rates by vaccine
sections.summary: Crude incidence rates based on 247 vaccinated deaths were read out, along with numbers of unvaccinated and medically ineligible individuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I am going to read out some crude incidence rates but, be mindful we are calculating these based on quite a small sample of 247 deaths of individuals who are vaccinated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: They are as follows: 79 deaths per 100,000 for non-fully vaccinated persons overall; 11 deaths per 100,000 for those vaccinated with Sinovac; 7.8 per 100,000 for Sinopharm; 6.2 per 100,000 for Pfizer-BioNTech and one per 100,000 for Moderna.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Around 132,000 individuals aged 18 and above remain unvaccinated, while around 300 persons are medically ineligible.

sections.label: Booster coverage and validity period
sections.summary: Booster coverage will expand over January, and full vaccination status has a validity period of 270 days.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Our booster coverage will continue to expand over the month of January.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: We have also set a validity period for full vaccination status of 270 days, as a strong signal to our population, "Please get your boosters promptly".

sections.label: COVID-19 bed capacity preparations
sections.summary: Preparations were made to ramp up capacity and manpower, with readiness to provide ICU, isolation and CTF beds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: We have made preparations to ramp up capacity and manpower of the Home Recovery Programme, Community Treatment Facilities (CTFs) and public hospitals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: We stand ready to provide up to 350 ICU beds, 2,000 isolation beds and 4,000 CTF beds for COVID-19 cases with a couple of weeks’ notice.

sections.label: VDS measures and children's coverage
sections.summary: Singapore introduced vaccination-differentiated measures instead of broad restrictions, but has no plans for VDS for children aged 12 and below, whose COVID-19 medical bills remain fully covered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: In recent months, instead of imposing across-the-board social restrictions, we introduced more vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS).

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: This is because unvaccinated individuals are at far higher risk of falling severely ill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: This group has consistently taken up two-thirds of our ICU beds, throughout the pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: The rest of society who have been vaccinated can also then live life more normally.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: However, there are, presently, no plans to introduce VDS for children aged 12 and below in community, public, preschool and school settings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: For now, children aged 12 and below who are Singapore Citizens, Permanent Residents or Long-Term Pass Holders and did not travel recently will continue to have their COVID-19 medical bills fully covered by the Government.
